pharm: A centrally acting analgesic structurally and pharmacologically distinct from opioids, NSAIDs, and paracetamol. It is thought to relieve pain mainly by inhibiting reuptake of serotonin, noradrenaline, and dopamine and by modulating glutamatergic (NMDA) transmission. It has anticholinergic and sympathomimetic properties but produces no respiratory depression and is not anti-inflammatory or antipyretic.

summary: Nefopam is a centrally acting non-opioid analgesic used (outside the United States, e.g. under EMA/SmPC and the BNF) for relief of acute and chronic pain such as post-operative, dental, musculoskeletal, traumatic, and cancer pain. It is NOT approved by the US FDA. It has marked anticholinergic and sympathomimetic activity, so it can cause dry mouth, urinary retention, tachycardia, sweating, nervousness, and at higher doses confusion, hallucinations and convulsions. It is contraindicated in patients with a history of convulsive (seizure) disorders and must not be given with monoamine oxidase inhibitors. Unlike opioids it does not cause respiratory depression but it has potential for dependence.
indications: Relief of acute pain, including post-operative pain and acute traumatic pain
Relief of chronic pain, including musculoskeletal pain and cancer pain
(Not an FDA-approved indication in the US; indications per EMA/SmPC and BNF)

moa: Nefopam is a benzoxazocine analgesic that is chemically and pharmacologically distinct from opioids, NSAIDs, and paracetamol. Its analgesic action is not fully defined but is attributed to inhibition of the reuptake of the monoamine neurotransmitters serotonin, noradrenaline (norepinephrine), and dopamine in the spinal cord and brain, together with modulation of glutamatergic transmission (including blockade of voltage-gated sodium and calcium channels and an effect on NMDA-receptor signalling). These central actions raise the nociceptive threshold without acting at opioid receptors, so nefopam produces no respiratory depression and does not relieve pain through anti-inflammatory or antipyretic mechanisms. It additionally has anticholinergic and sympathomimetic properties that account for many of its adverse effects.

Concomitant use of monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) - risk of severe hypertension/serotonergic crisis
Known hypersensitivity to nefopam or any excipient

Recent myocardial infarction (no clinical experience; sympathomimetic effects)

preg: Safety in human pregnancy has not been established and there are no adequate data. Nefopam should be avoided in pregnancy unless considered absolutely necessary and the benefit clearly outweighs the potential risk. (Per EMA/SmPC; not FDA-evaluated.)
lact: Nefopam is excreted in breast milk. Breast-feeding is contraindicated / should be avoided during treatment because of the potential for adverse effects in the infant. (Per EMA/SmPC.)
renal: Nefopam and its metabolites are eliminated largely via the kidneys, so excretion is impaired in renal insufficiency. Use with caution and reduce the daily dose in renal impairment. (Per SmPC; no formal FDA dosing exists.)
hepatic: Nefopam undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism, which may be impaired in liver disease leading to accumulation. Use with caution and reduce the dose in hepatic impairment. (Per SmPC.)

major: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) - contraindicated; risk of severe hypertension and serotonergic toxicity
Other agents lowering the seizure threshold - increased convulsion risk (nefopam can provoke seizures)
moderate: Other anticholinergic drugs (antihistamines, antimuscarinics) - additive antimuscarinic toxicity (dry mouth, retention, confusion)
CNS depressants / alcohol - additive sedation and dizziness
minor: May modestly potentiate effects of other centrally acting analgesics
interactions.food: Food has no clinically important effect on absorption; may be taken with or without food.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol - additive central nervous system depression, dizziness and sedation.
interactions.diagnostics: May cause false-positive results on urine immunoassays for benzodiazepines and opioids; urine may turn pink.

serious: Hallucinations and confusion (especially in the elderly)

counsel: This medicine treats pain but is not an opioid and is not anti-inflammatory
It may make your urine turn pink - this is harmless
It can cause a dry mouth, blurred vision, sweating, a fast heartbeat, or trouble passing urine - tell your doctor if these are troublesome
Do not drink alcohol while taking it, as it can make you drowsy or dizzy
Tell your doctor if you have epilepsy or seizures, take an MAOI antidepressant, or have glaucoma or prostate problems
Seek urgent help if you have a seizure, severe confusion or hallucinations, or a very fast or pounding heartbeat
Do not drive or operate machinery until you know how it affects you

Plasma Tmax ~1-3 hours after oral administration
Several hours; dosed three times daily
Store below 25 C; no special storage conditions required (per SmPC)
pearls: NOT FDA-approved in the US - clinical data here are drawn from the BNF, EMA/SmPC and WHO sources
Centrally acting non-opioid: no respiratory depression, but it is NOT anti-inflammatory or antipyretic
Contraindicated in patients with a seizure history and must never be combined with an MAOI
Anticholinergic - avoid or use cautiously in glaucoma, prostatic hypertrophy/urinary retention, and the elderly
Harmless pink discoloration of urine; can cause false-positive benzodiazepine/opioid urine screens
Overdose is characterized by convulsions, hallucinations and tachycardia - manage seizures with a benzodiazepine
missed: If a dose is missed, take it as soon as you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose, in which case skip the missed dose. Do not take two doses at once to make up for a missed dose.
overdose: Overdose produces neurological effects (agitation, hallucinations, convulsions, and at high doses coma) together with cardiovascular effects (tachycardia and other sympathomimetic/anticholinergic features). There is no specific antidote. Management is supportive: airway protection, activated charcoal if presentation is early, intravenous benzodiazepines (e.g. diazepam) to control seizures, and treatment of cardiovascular complications (e.g. beta-blockade for marked tachycardia) with close monitoring.
